title: How to Stop Puppy Biting: The Pause, Redirect, Reward Method
description: Puppy biting is normal but painful. Learn why puppies bite and a simple three-step method (pause, redirect, reward) that works without punishment.
excerpt: Sharp little teeth are normal. A gentle three-step method that works without punishment.
seoTitle: How to Stop Puppy Biting: 3-Step Method
imageAlt: Golden retriever puppy resting its head on its paws
html:
Sharp little teeth on your hands, ankles and trouser legs can make a new puppy feel like a tiny shark. It hurts, it is frustrating, and it can make you wonder whether something is wrong with your puppy. Nothing is. Mouthing is a normal part of how puppies explore and a normal part of teething, and it is very trainable with a calm, consistent approach.

Why do puppies bite?

Understanding the reason helps you pick the right response. Most puppy biting comes from a few simple causes:

  • Exploring. Puppies use their mouths to learn about the world, much like toddlers use their hands.
  • Teething. Chewing can feel good on sore gums while baby teeth are coming out and adult teeth are coming in.
  • Play. Puppies play with each other using their mouths, and your hands can look like a toy.
  • Overtired or overexcited. Biting often spikes late in the day, especially when a puppy has missed naps.
  • Attention. If biting makes you squeal, move or chase, some puppies learn that it works.

What is normal, and how long does it last?

Mouthy behavior is very common in the first months. Many puppies start losing their baby teeth at around four to six months, and chewing often continues for a while after that, though it differs from puppy to puppy. With consistent training, most puppies learn to be much gentler over weeks, not days. If you are unsure whether your puppy's biting is within the normal range, your vet or a qualified trainer can help.

The method: Pause, Redirect, Reward

Step 1: Pause

The moment teeth touch skin, stay calm and stop the game. Go still, or stand up and step away for a few seconds. No shouting, no hitting, no pinning the puppy down. The message is simple: teeth on skin makes the fun stop.

Step 2: Redirect

Offer an appropriate chew toy or tug toy. This shows your puppy what they can bite. Keep toys within reach in every room so you are never caught empty-handed.

Step 3: Reward

When your puppy chews the toy, praise warmly and give a treat when appropriate. Puppies repeat what pays off, so make the right choice the most rewarding one.

You will repeat this many times, and that is fine. Each calm repetition teaches the same lesson.

What to do in common situations

SituationTry this
Puppy bites your hands during playPause, hand a toy, restart the game when they chew the toy
Puppy grabs your trousers or socksStand still like a tree, then redirect to a toy
Puppy gets wild in the eveningCalm quiet time, a chew in the pen or crate, early bedtime
Puppy bites the leashStop, offer a treat, reward walking calmly beside you
Children get nippedAdults supervise, kids stay calm, give toys instead of hands

Make it easier

  • Keep several chew toys within reach in every room.
  • Plan naps. A well-rested puppy bites less.
  • Keep play sessions short and end them before your puppy gets wild.
  • Give frozen or safe chew options for teething, chosen to suit your puppy's size and age.
  • Use calm voices and slow movements around a mouthy puppy.
  • Give daily mental exercise such as sniffing walks and simple puzzle games, since a tired mind bites less.

Common mistakes that make biting worse

  1. Rough play that winds the puppy up.
  2. Waving hands or feet in front of the puppy's face.
  3. Punishing, which can create fear and mistrust.
  4. Inconsistency: allowing biting sometimes and not other times.
  5. Skipping rest and mental exercise.
  6. Letting children play unsupervised with a mouthy puppy.

A day that makes biting easier

Biting is much easier to manage when the day has a rhythm. A sample day for a young puppy might look like this:

  1. Morning: potty, breakfast, a short play session, then a nap.
  2. Midday: potty, a sniffing walk or simple puzzle, a chew, then rest.
  3. Afternoon: short training games with treats, then another nap.
  4. Evening: gentle play, a chew in a calm spot, potty and bedtime.

Puppies often need many more hours of sleep than owners expect. If biting is getting worse in the evening, an earlier, calmer wind-down is often the fix, not more play.

Games that teach gentle mouths

  • Trade. Offer a treat in exchange for what is in the mouth, then give the item back when appropriate. Your puppy learns that giving things up is rewarding.
  • Hand feeding. Feed a few meals from your hand so your puppy practices taking food gently.
  • Tug with rules. Short games with a toy, and a calm pause whenever teeth touch your hand. Start again when the puppy lets go.
  • Name and treat. Say your puppy's name, reward eye contact, and build a habit of checking in with you.

Teething relief ideas

If your puppy is chewing everything, soothe their gums safely. Many owners use chilled, not frozen-solid, chew toys, a damp knotted cloth under supervision, or a rubber chew designed for puppies. Avoid anything that can splinter or break into pieces, and ask your vet before offering frozen items to very small puppies. Supervise chewing, and replace worn toys.

Frequently asked questions

Should I hold my puppy's mouth closed?

No. Holding the mouth or pushing a hand down the throat can frighten a puppy and damage trust. Pause, redirect and reward instead.

Is yelping like another puppy a good idea?

A sharp sound can startle some puppies and excite others, so it does not work for every puppy. A calm pause and a toy is usually more reliable.

When does biting stop?

Most puppies become much gentler over the first months with steady training and plenty of rest. Teething and adolescence can bring phases of more chewing, so keep your routine going.

When to ask a professional

If biting is intense, comes with growling or stiff body language, or you are worried about safety, ask a qualified trainer or your veterinarian for help. Getting support early makes everything easier.
